lessons.title: Lesson 1: How much water does your crop need, and when?
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the thirstiest growth stages of your crop and check soil moisture by hand.
This lesson builds toward: For your main crop, you will name its thirstiest growth stages and check soil moisture at root depth by hand, deciding correctly whether to water or wait.
FAO's training manual on irrigation water needs explains that a crop's water need depends on three things: the climate, the type of crop, and its growth stage. Hot, sunny, dry and windy days make crops use more water; cool, cloudy, still days less. Tall, leafy crops use more than small ones.
Growth stage matters most for planning. A crop needs little water when small, the most during flowering and when grain or fruit is forming, and less as it ripens. Maize is hurt most by drought at tasselling and silking; tomatoes at flowering and fruit set; beans at flowering and pod fill. A dry spell at these stages costs the most yield.
Check the soil, not just the surface. Push a finger or a small stick into the soil near the roots, about 10 to 15 cm deep, or dig a small hole and squeeze a handful. If it holds together and feels moist, wait. If it crumbles and feels dry at root depth, it is time to water. Part of the rain that falls is lost to runoff or drains too deep; the part the crop can use is called effective rainfall.
Step by step:
- Write your crop and how many days from planting to harvest.
- Mark its thirstiest stages (for example maize: tasselling and silking).
- Each week, check the soil at root depth with a finger, stick or hole.
- Note the weather: hot, windy, dry days mean more water use.
- Water before the soil at root depth dries out, especially at the thirsty stages.
Words to know:
- Crop water need: the amount of water a crop uses to grow well.
- Growth stage: a period in a crop's life, such as seedling, flowering or ripening.
- Effective rainfall: the part of the rain that stays in the root zone and the crop can use.
- Root zone: the layer of soil where most of the crop's roots are.
Official sources:
- FAO Irrigation Water Management Training Manual No. 3: Irrigation Water Needs
Try it now: For one crop you grow, write the weeks after planting when it reaches its thirstiest stages. Then check your soil at root depth today with a finger, stick or small hole and write: moist or dry.
You can now say when your crop needs water most and check soil moisture at root depth.

check.q: When do beans need water most?
check.why: Beans are hurt most by drought at flowering and pod fill.

check.q: You dig a small hole near the roots. The soil crumbles and feels dry at that depth. What do you do?
check.why: If the soil crumbles and feels dry at root depth, it is time to water.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Harvesting rainwater from roofs and fields
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Work out how much rain your roof can collect and choose a field method to keep rain on your land.
This lesson builds toward: For your roof and land, you will estimate how much rain a roof can collect and choose a field method to keep rain on your land, using about 1 litre per square metre for every millimetre of rain, and planning on less.
Water harvesting means catching rain where it falls or runs, and keeping it for crops, animals or the home. FAO's water harvesting manual describes many field methods used in dry areas: planting pits (such as zai pits), semi-circular bunds, contour ridges, small diamond-shaped catchments around trees (negarim) and stone bunds.
Roof catchment is the simplest start. Every 1 millimetre of rain on 1 square metre of roof gives about 1 litre of water. A roof of 50 square metres in a place with 600 mm of rain a year can give up to 30,000 litres a year, though some is always lost, so plan on less. Fit gutters, a first-flush pipe that throws away the first dirty water, and a covered tank.
Runoff from roads, paths and slopes can be led into a lined water pan or farm pond. Planting pits filled with compost or manure catch rain right at the roots of maize, sorghum or young fruit trees. Start small and watch where water flows on your land in the next storm.
Step by step:
- Measure your roof: length times width in metres.
- Find your yearly rainfall from your weather service or extension officer.
- Multiply roof area by rainfall in mm to get litres, then plan on less for losses.
- Fit gutters, a first-flush pipe and a covered tank.
- Choose one field method (pits, bunds or contour ridges) for one plot.
Words to know:
- Water harvesting: catching and keeping rainwater or runoff for later use.
- Roof catchment: collecting rain from a roof through gutters into a tank.
- First flush: a pipe that throws away the first, dirtiest rain from the roof.
- Zai pit: a small planting pit filled with manure that catches rain at the roots.
Official sources:
- FAO: Water Harvesting, a manual for the design and construction of water harvesting schemes for plant production
Try it now: Measure your house or store roof and find your yearly rainfall. Work out how many litres it could collect in a year. Use your phone calculator, or ask a phone AI assistant to check your sum.
You can now estimate how much rainwater you can harvest and choose a field method to keep rain on your land.

check.q: Which is a field method that keeps rain on your land?
options: Ploughing up and down the slope
check.why: Planting pits, bunds and contour ridges catch rain where it falls.

check.q: In the next storm, water rushes along your farm road. What could you do with it?
options: Let it wash into the river
Lead it into a lined water pan or farm pond
Dig a hole in the middle of the road
check.why: Runoff from roads and paths can be led into a lined water pan or pond for later use.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Storing water safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Choose a water store and keep it clean, covered and legal.
This lesson builds toward: For harvested water, you will choose a water store and keep it clean, covered and legal, with the store covered or fenced and any permit checked.
Common stores are plastic or ferro-cement tanks, underground tanks, and water pans or farm ponds. Ponds lose a lot of water into the ground unless they are lined (for example with a dam liner) and a lot to the sun unless shaded or covered.
Keep stored water clean and safe. Cover tanks and ponds to keep out dirt, animals and children, and to stop mosquitoes breeding. Fence ponds. Clean gutters and tanks before the rains. Water for drinking needs more care than water for crops; ask your health office how to treat it.
Bigger water use may need a permit. In Kenya, the Water Resources Authority (WRA) regulates water use and issues permits, for example for boreholes and pumping from rivers. Other countries have their own water authorities. Check before you drill, dam or pump.
Step by step:
- Decide what the water is for: crops, animals or home.
- Choose a store: tank, underground tank, or lined pond.
- Cover it and fence ponds.
- Clean gutters and tanks before each rainy season.
- Before drilling or pumping from a river, check with your water authority.
Words to know:
- Water pan: a dug pond that collects runoff.
- Dam liner: a strong plastic sheet that stops a pond leaking into the ground.
- Permit: official permission to use or take water.
Official sources:
- Water Resources Authority, Kenya (water use permits)
Try it now: Write which store suits your farm and your budget, how you will cover and fence it, and the name of the office in your country that you would ask before drilling or pumping.
You can now choose a water store, keep it safe, and know when you need a permit.

check.q: Which store loses the most water unless it is lined and covered?
check.why: Ponds lose water into the ground unless lined, and to the sun unless shaded or covered.

check.q: You want to use some stored rainwater for drinking. What do you do?
options: Drink it straight from the pond
Ask your health office how to treat it
check.why: Drinking water needs more care than water for crops; ask the health office how to treat it.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Low-cost drip irrigation
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Set up and look after a bucket or drum drip kit for a small plot.
This lesson builds toward: For a plot of about 100 to 500 square metres, you will set up and look after a gravity drip kit, with the drum at least 1 metre high, a clean filter and no blocked emitters.
Drip irrigation puts water slowly at the base of each plant through thin pipes with small holes (emitters). Less water is lost to the sun and wind, leaves stay dry so there is less disease, and weeds between rows get less water.
FAO's handbook on pressurized irrigation describes low-cost family drip systems for plots of about 100 to 500 square metres: a bucket or drum raised at least 1 metre above the beds feeds a filter, a main pipe and drip lines along each row. Gravity gives the pressure, so no pump is needed to run it. Kits are sold by agro-dealers and irrigation suppliers; compare prices and ask for spare parts.
Clogging is the main problem. Use clean water, keep the filter in place and clean it often, and flush the ends of the drip lines regularly. Cover the soil with mulch over the drip lines to cut evaporation further. Check each emitter is dripping; a dry plant usually means a blocked hole.
Step by step:
- Level the beds and lay drip lines along each row of plants.
- Raise the bucket or drum on a stand at least 1 metre above the beds.
- Connect drum, tap, filter, main pipe and drip lines; close the line ends.
- Fill with clean water, open the tap and check every emitter drips.
- Mulch over the lines.
- Clean the filter and flush line ends every week or two.
Words to know:
- Drip irrigation: watering plants drop by drop at the roots through thin pipes.
- Emitter: the small hole or dripper that lets water out near each plant.
- Filter: a screen that stops dirt from blocking the emitters.
- Gravity-fed: pushed by the height of the water tank, not by a pump.
Official sources:
- FAO: Technical handbook on pressurized irrigation techniques (includes low-cost family drip systems)
Try it now: Sketch a drip layout for a small plot: where the drum stands (at least 1 m high), the filter, the main pipe and each drip line. Then ask two suppliers or agro-dealers the price of a kit for that size and write both down.
You can now set up, run and look after a low-cost gravity drip kit.

check.q: What is an emitter on a drip line?
options: A small hole or dripper that lets water out at each plant
check.why: Emitters are the small holes that drip water at the base of each plant.

check.q: Your water comes from a muddy pond. How do you protect your drip kit?
options: Keep the filter in place, clean it often and flush the line ends
Remove the filter so water flows faster
Run the kit only at noon
check.why: Clean water, a clean filter and regular flushing prevent clogging, the main drip problem.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Scheduling: without waterlogging or salt
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a weekly watering schedule and spot waterlogging and salt build-up early.
This lesson builds toward: Over a growing season, you will make a weekly watering schedule and spot waterlogging and salt build-up early, checking the soil before each watering.
A schedule answers two questions: when to water and how much. Water early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when less is lost to the sun. Water more often during hot, windy weather and the thirsty stages, and skip watering after good rain. Keep checking the soil at root depth; the schedule is a guide, the soil has the final word.
Too much water is as harmful as too little. Waterlogged soil has no air for roots: plants turn yellow and wilt even though the soil is wet, and roots rot. Signs are standing water, a sour smell and yellowing. Water less, open drains, and use raised beds or ridges on heavy clay.
FAO explains that salt builds up when irrigation water brings in more salt than drains away, and that over-irrigation and poor drainage are common causes. Watch for a white crust on the soil, leaf edges that burn, and poor growth. Good drainage, mulch and enough (not too much) water help. If you see these signs, or use borehole water in a dry area, ask your extension officer or soil lab to test the water and soil.
Step by step:
- Write a weekly plan: which days, morning or evening, how long.
- Water more at thirsty stages and in hot, windy weeks.
- Skip watering after good rain.
- Check soil at root depth before each watering.
- Look for standing water, sour smell and yellowing (waterlogging).
- Look for a white crust and burnt leaf edges (salt); ask for a water and soil test.
Words to know:
- Irrigation schedule: a plan for when and how much to water.
- Waterlogging: soil so full of water that roots get no air.
- Salinity: too much salt in the soil or water, which harms crops.
- Drainage: the way extra water leaves the soil.
Official sources:
- FAO Irrigation Water Management Training Manual No. 3: Irrigation Water Needs
- FAO: Water quality for agriculture (salinity, leaching and drainage)
Try it now: Write a one-week watering schedule for one crop: days, time of day and how long. Next to it, write the two warning signs of waterlogging and the two of salt build-up you will look for each time you water.
You can now schedule irrigation and spot waterlogging and salt build-up before they ruin a crop.

check.q: What does a watering schedule decide?
options: When to water and how much
check.why: A schedule answers when to water and how much, and the soil check has the final word.

check.q: You water with borehole water in a dry area, and growth gets poorer each season. What do you do?
options: Ask your extension officer or a soil lab to test the water and soil
check.why: Borehole water in dry areas can bring salt; a water and soil test shows what is wrong.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Choosing a pump, including solar pumps
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare treadle, fuel and solar pumps and list what to ask a supplier.
This lesson builds toward: When water must be lifted or moved, you will compare treadle, fuel and solar pumps and list what to ask a supplier, giving the daily water need, lift and distance, and pumping only what the crop needs.
If water is below or far from your plot, you need a pump. Treadle and hand pumps are cheap and use your own effort, good for small plots near shallow water. Petrol and diesel pumps are cheap to buy and move easily, but fuel and repairs cost money every week. Solar pumps cost more to buy but use free sunlight, so running costs are very low.
To choose, know three things: how much water you need each day, how high the water must be lifted (from the water level to the tank or field), and how far it must travel. A supplier needs these to size the pump. A pump that is too small will not give enough water; one that is too big wastes money.
FAO points out a risk with solar pumps: because each extra hour of pumping is free, farmers may pump more than the river or groundwater can sustain. Pump only what your crop needs, share water fairly with neighbours, and follow your water authority's rules. Keep panels clean and secure, and ask for a warranty, spare parts and after-sales service in writing. Some suppliers offer pay-as-you-go plans; read the full price and terms first.
Step by step:
- Work out water needed per day for your plot.
- Measure lift: from water level to tank or field.
- Measure distance from source to plot.
- Compare treadle, fuel and solar on purchase cost, running cost and work.
- Ask the supplier for sizing, warranty, spares and service in writing.
- Check water permits before pumping from a river or borehole.
Words to know:
- Treadle pump: a foot-powered pump for lifting water from shallow sources.
- Solar pump: a pump powered by solar panels.
- Lift (head): how high the pump must raise the water.
- Over-abstraction: taking more water from a river or underground than nature puts back.
Official sources:
- FAO: Positive prospects for solar-powered irrigation systems
- Water Resources Authority, Kenya (water use permits)
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page irrigation plan. Include your crop's thirsty stages, your water source and storage, your drip or other system, a weekly schedule, how you will avoid waterlogging and salt, and the pump you would choose with your lift, distance and daily water need.
You can now choose the right kind of pump and put together a full irrigation plan for a small plot.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Crop and thirsty stages The crop's thirstiest stages are missing or wrong. Names the crop and its thirstiest growth stages, with how the soil will be checked. Notes the planting date so the thirsty stages are on the calendar. Water source and storage No water source, or no estimate of how much can be stored. Water source, a roof or runoff estimate, and a covered store, with any permit checked. Includes a field method such as planting pits to keep rain on the land. Irrigation system No system, or no plan to prevent clogging. A drip or other system that fits the plot, with drum height, filter and flushing. Includes mulch over the lines and a list of spare parts. Schedule and soil checks No schedule, or watering at noon with no soil check. A weekly schedule with time of day, more water at thirsty stages, and a soil check before watering. Says what to do after good rain and in hot, windy weeks. Waterlogging and salt No plan for waterlogging or salt. Signs to watch for and steps such as drains, raised beds and not over-watering. Plans a water and soil test if using borehole water in a dry area. Pump choice No pump choice, or no reason. A pump type with its reason, the daily water need, lift and distance. Lists warranty, spare parts and service to ask for in writing. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and check it again.

check.q: Which pump uses your own effort and suits a small plot near shallow water?
check.why: Treadle and hand pumps are cheap and suit small plots near shallow water.

check.q: Your new solar pump can run all day for free, but the river is getting low. What do you do?
options: Pump all day because it is free
Pump only what the crop needs and share water fairly with neighbours
check.why: Free pumping can take too much water; pump only what the crop needs and follow the water authority's rules.
